minio: own container, not capped (our lines only)
network: docker network fxbench 172.31.77.0/24; client on the host
server_help:
Usage: mongo-server [OPTIONS]

Options:
      --listen <LISTEN>
          Address to listen on [default: 127.0.0.1:27018]
      --idle-secs <IDLE_SECS>
          Close a database's tenant after this many idle seconds [default: 60]
      --endpoint <ENDPOINT>
          S3 endpoint URL, only for S3-compatible services such as MinIO (also read from AWS_ENDPOINT). Empty: AWS itself. An `http://` endpoint switches plain HTTP on [default: ""]
      --region <REGION>
          S3 region (also read from AWS_REGION or AWS_DEFAULT_REGION). With `--store s3` one of the three must be set: the engine has no region of its own
      --bucket <BUCKET>
          [default: bench]
      --no-maintenance
          Do not run the background compaction and GC loops (also disables the L0 guard)
      --lease-ttl-secs <LEASE_TTL_SECS>
          Tenant lease time-to-live; leases of open tenants are renewed every third of it, and a crashed process's tenants can be taken over once it has passed [default: 30]
      --holder <HOLDER>
          Lease holder id (default: a unique id per process start)
      --ttl-sweep-secs <TTL_SWEEP_SECS>
          Remove expired TTL documents of tenants that are open as writers this often [default: 60]
      --ttl-wake-sleeping
          Wake sleeping tenants to remove their expired documents (off by default). Off: expired documents are hidden on every read and removed at the tenant's next natural writer session; nothing is woken, no expiry hint is written at close and no maintenance pass lists anything. On: a maintenance pass (one LIST per pass) wakes tenants whose documents are due, each at most once per `--ttl-min-gap-secs`
      --ttl-maintenance-secs <TTL_MAINTENANCE_SECS>
          With `--ttl-wake-sleeping`: every this often, look for sleeping tenants with expired documents and wake due ones [default: 60]
      --ttl-min-gap-secs <TTL_MIN_GAP_SECS>
          Do not wake the same sleeping tenant for expiry more often than this [default: 3600]
      --ttl-max-wakes <TTL_MAX_WAKES>
          At most this many sleeping tenants are woken for expiry per maintenance pass [default: 20]
      --replica-set <REPLICA_SET>
          Replica-set name reported by `hello`. Drivers allow multi-document transactions and change streams only on replica sets, so set it (with `--advertise`) when an application needs them; empty (default) is a standalone server, which is what clients that connect by another host name or address expect [default: ""]
      --advertise <ADVERTISE>
          Address advertised in `hello.hosts` / `me`; must match the host:port clients connect to (default `localhost:<listen port>`)
      --no-ttl
          Do not run the TTL sweeps (expired documents stay hidden but are not removed)
      --wal-flush-ms <WAL_FLUSH_MS>
          WAL flush interval in milliseconds. 0 (default) keeps the baseline: slatedb's 100 ms periodic flush plus an explicit flush after every write batch, so a write is acknowledged as soon as its WAL object is durable. A value above 0 sets the periodic interval and drops the explicit flush: a write is acknowledged (durable) at the next flush, up to one interval later, and concurrent writes to a tenant share one WAL object [default: 0]
      --ack-before-durable
          Acknowledge writes before they are durable (they become durable at the next periodic flush). Unsafe: a crash can lose acknowledged writes. For measuring the durability trade-off only; use with --wal-flush-ms
      --store <STORE>
          Object store: `s3` (the endpoint above), `local` (a directory, see --local-dir) or `memory` [default: s3]
      --local-dir <LOCAL_DIR>
          [default: /tmp/mongo-server-store]
      --max-concurrent-wakes <MAX_CONCURRENT_WAKES>
          Cold wakes allowed at once; more queue (0 = unlimited). Measured with 500 databases waking together after a restart (MinIO, 2 CPUs, results-round3.md): first request p50/p99 2.7/16.4 s with 8, 3.9/12.1 s with 32, 6.1/8.6 s with 128, 6.3/9.5 s without a limit. 128 gives the shortest tail, which is what a customer waits for [default: 128]
      --memtable-max-mb <MEMTABLE_MAX_MB>
          Memtable size in MiB (slatedb's own estimate of the data) at which a writer flushes it to an L0 SST (slatedb's default is 64 MiB per database). The process memory a memtable holds is about 4 times this estimate for 1 KB documents (results-round3.md). 2 bounded the memory better but, on real S3, a database at 100 writes/s then flushed L0 so often that its writes stalled on compaction (p99 2-3 s, request cost doubled); 8 had no such stall (results-round3.md, part E). 0 = slatedb's default [default: 8]
      --memtable-max-age-secs <MEMTABLE_MAX_AGE_SECS>
          A writer flushes its memtable to an L0 SST once its oldest unflushed write is this old, in seconds (0 = only when the memtable is full or after slatedb's 4096 WAL flushes). Measured (mem-growth branch, 50 databases at 2 writes/s): the memtables of slowly written databases were most of the memory that grew with the writes. A database written fast fills its memtable before this age and is not affected; a slow one gets at most one more L0 SST per interval [default: 600]
      --cache-flushed-blocks <CACHE_FLUSHED_BLOCKS>
          Also keep the data blocks of the L0 SSTs a writer flushes in the shared block cache (slatedb's default). Off: those blocks filled the cache with data nobody had read and, after the database closed, could never be read again (new cache scope per open). Blocks are still cached when read [default: false] [possible values: true, false]
      --compaction-warm <COMPACTION_WARM>
          After a compaction pass of an open database, read into the shared block cache the new blocks that hold the keys of the blocks it had cached, before the database switches to the new manifest (`src/warm.rs`). Off: every compaction cooled the cache, the hot reads went back to object storage (M27: 0% of the hot reads served by the cache after a pass) [default: true] [possible values: true, false]
      --compaction-warm-ms <COMPACTION_WARM_MS>
          Longest warm-up after one compaction pass, in milliseconds; past it the warm-up stops where it is (what it read stays in the cache) and the database switches to the new manifest anyway [default: 3000]
      --compaction-warm-concurrency <COMPACTION_WARM_CONCURRENCY>
          Warm-up reads in flight at once per warm-up (`warm_sst` calls of 2 range GETs each). The rate of all warm-ups together is bounded by `--compaction-warm-gets-per-sec` [default: 128]
      --compaction-warm-max-key-mb <COMPACTION_WARM_MAX_KEY_MB>
          Most MB of hot keys one warm-up keeps in memory; past it only a part of the hot blocks is warmed [default: 32]
      --compaction-warm-gets-per-sec <COMPACTION_WARM_GETS_PER_SEC>
          Most warm-up GETs per second for the whole process, all compaction warm-ups together (one shared token bucket; 0 = no limit). Under S3's 5,500 GET/s of one partition with room for the other requests of the same prefixes [default: 3000]
      --cursor-timeout-secs <CURSOR_TIMEOUT_SECS>
          A cursor (find, aggregate, tailable, change stream) that no getMore used for this long is closed and its buffered results freed, as mongod's `cursorTimeoutMillis` (10 minutes). Before, an abandoned cursor stayed until the process stopped. 0 = never [default: 600]
      --block-cache-mb <BLOCK_CACHE_MB>
          One block cache shared by every open database, in MiB (slatedb's default is a 512 MiB cache per open database, with no limit across databases: the memory then grew with the data read by each database) [default: 256]
      --meta-cache-mb <META_CACHE_MB>
          One metadata cache (SST indexes and filters) shared by every open database, in MiB (slatedb's default: 128 MiB per database) [default: 64]
      --waiter-tools
          The waiter's tools (T1): the two-floor counter (RAM + local disk) with the maps pinned (SST indexes and filters, collection indexes, metadata), one trip per cold read, read-ahead on a signal. Replaces --block-cache-mb and --meta-cache-mb. Off by default until reviewed
      --counter-ram-pct <COUNTER_RAM_PCT>
          RAM of the counter, in percent of the machine's (or cgroup's) memory (--waiter-tools) [default: 50]
      --counter-ram-mb <COUNTER_RAM_MB>
          RAM of the counter in MiB, instead of the percentage (0 = use the percentage) [default: 0]
      --counter-disk-dir <COUNTER_DISK_DIR>
          Directory of the counter's disk floor (local NVMe). Empty = no disk floor. Emptied at start [default: ""]
      --counter-disk-gb <COUNTER_DISK_GB>
          Size of the disk floor in GiB (0 = 80% of the free space of its file system at start) [default: 0]
      --split-get-min-kb <SPLIT_GET_MIN_KB>
          Ranged GETs at least this long (KiB) are sent as parallel pieces (0 = never; --waiter-tools) [default: 512]
      --split-get-piece-kb <SPLIT_GET_PIECE_KB>
          Size of one piece of a split GET, KiB [default: 256]
      --hedge-after-ms <HEDGE_AFTER_MS>
          Hedged reads (--waiter-tools): a ranged GET not answered after this many ms is sent again, first answer wins (0 = off) [default: 0]
      --filter-bits-per-key <FILTER_BITS_PER_KEY>
          Bloom filter bits per key of new SSTs (slatedb's default 10). More bits, fewer false positives: a cold point read then waits for one read, not two in a row (T1) [default: 10]
      --next-block-kb <NEXT_BLOCK_KB>
          Next-block read-along (--waiter-tools): a small ranged GET of an SST also brings this many KiB after it (T1: slatedb reads the block before a key that starts a block first; this keeps both in one trip). 0 = off [default: 8]
      --read-ahead-docs <READ_AHEAD_DOCS>
          Read ahead on a signal (T1, prefetch.rs): the first indexed read of a key prefix brings this many more entries' documents in the background, and a read that goes past them brings the next ones. 0 = off [default: 200]
      --change-log-max-mb <CHANGE_LOG_MAX_MB>
          Memory the change-stream event log may hold, in MiB (estimated). Older events are dropped first; a resume token older than the oldest event kept fails with ChangeStreamHistoryLost. The log keeps whole documents, so without this limit every write grew the process by ~4 KB until 100 000 events were held [default: 32]
      --relaxed-flush-ms <RELAXED_FLUSH_MS>
          Relaxed durability for databases without their own setting (`PUT /v1/databases/{db}/durability`), in milliseconds: 0 (default) = off, otherwise 1000 to 10000. A write with write concern `{w: 1, j: false}` to such a database is acknowledged before it is durable and becomes durable within this interval (lost if the process dies first); `j: true`, `w: "majority"` and writes without a write concern stay durable before the acknowledgement [default: 0]
      --adaptive-group-commit <ADAPTIVE_GROUP_COMMIT>
          Adaptive group commit: the first write of a group waits a short window (half the database's average flush time, at most --adaptive-group-commit-max-us) when more writes of the same database are expected within it, so they share one WAL object. A database written rarely never waits [default: false] [possible values: true, false]
      --adaptive-group-commit-max-us <ADAPTIVE_GROUP_COMMIT_MAX_US>
          [default: 5000]
      --local-log-dir <LOCAL_LOG_DIR>
          PROTOTYPE, off by default: a durable log in this local directory. Writes are acknowledged after the log's fsync and reach object storage in blocks every --local-log-upload-secs; a restart applies the records not yet uploaded. Losing the disk loses up to that interval of acknowledged writes of every database. See locallog.rs [default: ""]
      --local-log-upload-secs <LOCAL_LOG_UPLOAD_SECS>
          [default: 30]
      --quaderno <QUADERNO>
          Q8d, off by default: the replicated log (quaderno, proto/quaderno) as the durability of every write, at these three copies (`a:p,b:p,c:p`). A write is acknowledged when 2 copies of 3 have its record; object storage gets it every --local-log-upload-secs (1 to 60 here), then the log drops it. A restart (on any machine) reads back from the log what object storage does not have yet. --local-log-dir, if set, only keeps conflicting records. See qlog.rs [default: ""]
      --quaderno-id <QUADERNO_ID>
          Name of the log in the markers stored with the data (the same for every engine that uses this log) [default: cell1]
      --agent-lane <AGENT_LANE>
          PROTOTYPE, off by default: collections on the agent lane, comma-separated `database.collection` patterns (`*` matches any run of characters), e.g. `*.checkpoints,*.checkpoint_writes`. Their writes skip the local and replicated log and are acknowledged once the WAL object holding them is in object storage. A collection can also be put on the lane with `collMod` / `create` and the option `fenvixAgentLane: true`. See agentlane.rs [default: ""]
      --agent-lane-window-ms <AGENT_LANE_WINDOW_MS>
          Agent lane: the batch window (ms). The first write of a batch waits this long for others to share its PUT; a transaction's commit does not wait [default: 100]
      --agent-lane-follow <AGENT_LANE_FOLLOW>
          Agent lane: follow these databases' WAL objects in object storage (comma-separated names), as a warm spare does, so that a takeover replays the last batches from memory instead of reading them one by one. See agentlane.rs [default: ""]
      --local-log-replay-timeout-secs <LOCAL_LOG_REPLAY_TIMEOUT_SECS>
          Local log: the restart gives up on replaying one database after this long (its records are kept for the next restart) so that one stuck database (its S3 requests hanging or retried) does not keep the whole server down [default: 120]
      --fair-lag-ms <FAIR_LAG_MS>
          Fair queue between databases, only while the server is saturated: when the runtime runs a 10 ms timer late by more than this (moving average, ms), new commands wait in their database's queue and start in turn (wakes first) as others finish; below it every command starts at once. 0 = off. See fair.rs [default: 2]
      --fair-max-inflight <FAIR_MAX_INFLIGHT>
          While saturated (see --fair-lag-ms), at most this many commands run at once; the others wait in turn (0 = 8 per CPU) [default: 0]
      --fair-max-flushing <FAIR_MAX_FLUSHING>
          While saturated, at most this many commands at once have their written data flushed (the flush is CPU work in the database's background tasks); the others wait in turn, least used databases first (0 = 4 per CPU) [default: 0]
      --db-max-inflight <DB_MAX_INFLIGHT>
          Safety limit per database, only against runaway clients: commands running or queued at once (0 = none) [default: 10000]
      --db-max-rate <DB_MAX_RATE>
          Safety limit per database, only against runaway clients: commands in one second (0 = none) [default: 100000]
      --db-quota-pts <DB_QUOTA_PTS>
          Quota per database in points per second (the unit of fair.rs: CPU, bytes written and read, S3 requests), for databases without their own (PUT /v1/databases/{db}/quota). Over it a database's commands wait in its own queue. 0 = none [default: 0]
      --db-burst-pts <DB_BURST_PTS>
          Burst credit per database in points: how far a database may go over its quota for a while (0 = 10 s of quota) [default: 0]
      --db-quota-queue <DB_QUOTA_QUEUE>
          Commands of one database that may wait over its quota; beyond, a new one gets the retryable error 462 at once [default: 256]
      --unit-weights <UNIT_WEIGHTS>
          Weights of the unit, points per: CPU ms, KiB written, KiB read, S3 PUT-class request, S3 GET-class request (empty = defaults, see fair.rs) [default: ""]
      --js-command-max-ms <JS_COMMAND_MAX_MS>
          Longest total time one command may spend running JavaScript ($where, $function, $accumulator, mapReduce), in ms; over it the command fails with error 50 MaxTimeMSExpired. 0 = no limit (each call still has internalQueryJavaScriptFnTimeoutMillis) [default: 30000]
      --unsafe-skip-ownership-checks
          Test control only: never treat a lease as expired or lost. Demonstrates what the ownership checks prevent
      --serialize-reads
          Run reads of one tenant one at a time like writes (the behaviour before concurrent reads). By default reads of one tenant share the entry lock and run concurrently; writes and tenant state changes are exclusive
      --no-leases
          Do not use leases (single process only; for stores without conditional update, e.g. --store local)
      --no-group-commit
          Wait for each write's own flush while holding the tenant lock (the behaviour before group commit: one WAL object per write). By default writes arriving while a flush is in flight share the next WAL object
      --writer-poll-secs <WRITER_POLL_SECS>
          Seconds between manifest reads of an open writer (it learns of compactions, and retries a memtable flush that stalled on a full L0, at this pace). One LIST and one GET per open writer per interval: 60 s is ~86 000 requests a month per database open for writing (30 s, the old default, twice that). Must stay below --sst-gc-min-unref-secs [default: 60]
      --process-lease [<PROCESS_LEASE>]
          One lease per process (`processes/{holder}/_lease`, renewed every third of the ttl) plus a per-database owner record written when the database is opened, instead of one lease object renewed per open database (6 PUT per minute for every open database with the default ttl): an open database then costs no lease request. On by default; `--process-lease false` goes back to one lease per database. Every process sharing the bucket should use the same setting (a mix is safe, see lease.rs: each mode refuses the other's live records) [default: true] [possible values: true, false]
      --wal-gc-secs <WAL_GC_SECS>
          Seconds between WAL garbage-collection passes over an open writer that is being written (0 = off, WAL objects then stay until the tenant has been idle and is collected as a whole) [default: 20]
      --group-commit-window-ms <GROUP_COMMIT_WINDOW_MS>
          Group commit window in milliseconds (fractions allowed): the first write of a group waits this long before flushing so that more writes can share the WAL object. 0 (default) flushes at once [default: 0]
      --durable-reads <DURABLE_READS>
          Reads see only durable data (default true). `--durable-reads false`: reads may see writes that are staged and waiting for their group flush (they can disappear if the process dies before the flush) [default: true] [possible values: true, false]
      --metadata-cache <METADATA_CACHE>
          Keep the collection list, index definitions and collection options of open databases in memory (default true; see `dbs::META_CACHE`). `--metadata-cache false` reads them from storage on every command, as before [default: true] [possible values: true, false]
      --l0-max-ssts <L0_MAX_SSTS>
          Test control: slatedb's `l0_max_ssts` for writers (default 8, 0 keeps it). Lowering it makes the stalled-flush shutdown fallback reachable with a modest number of writes [default: 0]
      --wal-gc-mode <WAL_GC_MODE>
          How the WAL cleanup of an open writer works: `bulk` (default: remembers where it stopped, bulk deletes), `single` (the same with one DELETE per object), `slatedb` (slatedb's own pass: lists the whole WAL directory, one DELETE per object) or `list-only` (that listing without deleting; profiling only, bounds nothing) [default: bulk]
      --sst-gc-secs <SST_GC_SECS>
          Seconds between cleanups of the compacted SSTs and old manifests of an open writer (0 = off: they stay until the tenant closes) [default: 60]
      --sst-gc-min-unref-secs <SST_GC_MIN_UNREF_SECS>
          Seconds an SST or manifest must have been seen unreferenced before it is deleted (must exceed --writer-poll-secs, the staleness of a live writer's view of the manifest) [default: 120]
      --gc-control-delete-live
          Test control, unsafe: the SST cleanup also deletes the oldest SST the manifest still references
      --l0-sst-bytes <L0_SST_BYTES>
          Test control: memtable size at which a writer flushes it to an L0 SST (slatedb default 64 MiB; 0 keeps it) [default: 0]
      --group-commit-adaptive
          With --group-commit-window-ms: wait for the window only while another write of the tenant is still on its way to the flush; flush at once when none is (so a lone writer never waits). Without it the window is always waited
      --log-commands
          Log every command name and database to stderr
      --admin-listen <ADMIN_LISTEN>
          Address of the admin HTTP interface (off when not set). Needs a token; plain HTTP, so bind it to a private interface or put a TLS terminator in front
      --admin-token <ADMIN_TOKEN>
          Bearer token of the admin interface (at least 16 characters). Prefer `--admin-token-file` or the `MONGO_ADMIN_TOKEN` environment variable: command lines are visible to other users
      --admin-token-file <ADMIN_TOKEN_FILE>
          
      --retention-window-secs <RETENTION_WINDOW_SECS>
          Retention window (seconds) of databases without their own setting; 0 keeps no restore points [default: 0]
      --retention-interval-secs <RETENTION_INTERVAL_SECS>
          A new restore point is taken at most this often per database (and only if it was written since the last one) [default: 600]
      --retention-prune-secs <RETENTION_PRUNE_SECS>
          Expired restore points of sleeping databases are removed this often (slatedb's garbage collector does it for databases that are written) [default: 600]
      --usage-flush-secs <USAGE_FLUSH_SECS>
          Usage counters are written to the bucket this often (and at shutdown): one PUT per database used in the interval (60 s, the old default, was ~43 000 PUT a month for a database in use all the time; 300 s is a fifth of that) [default: 300]
      --pin-lease-ttl-secs <PIN_LEASE_TTL_SECS>
          Keep-awake leases last this long and are renewed every third of it [default: 30]
      --export-ttl-secs <EXPORT_TTL_SECS>
          Export snapshots expire after this long (their checkpoint is released then) [default: 86400]
      --no-ctl-recovery
          Skip the recovery of interrupted fork / restore / erase operations at start (test control only)
      --trusted-networks <TRUSTED_NETWORKS>
          Networks that skip the per-database allow lists, the authentication blocks and the per-address connection limit (comma-separated CIDRs; an empty value trusts nothing). Meant for the processes on the same host (control plane, Data Explorer): loopback, and the host's container network if they run in containers, e.g. `127.0.0.0/8,::1/128,172.17.0.0/16`. Never put a network through which outside clients arrive here [default: 127.0.0.0/8,::1/128]
      --auth-fail-max <AUTH_FAIL_MAX>
          Failed authentications from one address within --auth-fail-window-secs that block the address on every database (the failure that reaches the number starts the block; 0: never). High on purpose: a platform with one database per customer connects from few addresses, and one wrong password rotation must not block all its databases [default: 100]
      --auth-fail-max-per-db <AUTH_FAIL_MAX_PER_DB>
          Failed authentications from one address on one database within --auth-fail-window-secs that block the address on that database only (0: never) [default: 5]
      --auth-fail-window-secs <AUTH_FAIL_WINDOW_SECS>
          Length of the sliding window, in seconds, in which failed authentications are counted for both thresholds [default: 60]
      --auth-block-secs <AUTH_BLOCK_SECS>
          Length of a first block, in seconds; every new block of the same address (or address and database) doubles it [default: 300]
      --auth-block-max-secs <AUTH_BLOCK_MAX_SECS>
          Longest block, in seconds (the doubling stops here) [default: 3600]
      --auth-block-forget-secs <AUTH_BLOCK_FORGET_SECS>
          Without a new block for this many seconds, the doubling starts again from --auth-block-secs [default: 86400]
      --max-conns-per-ip <MAX_CONNS_PER_IP>
          Connections at once from one address, authenticated or not (0: no limit, the default). Further connections are closed at once. Off by default: serverless platforms reach the engine from a few shared addresses (see the module doc) [default: 0]
      --max-conns <MAX_CONNS>
          Connections at once in this process, from every address (like mongod's net.maxIncomingConnections). Further connections are closed at once, before TLS; trusted addresses are counted but never refused. 0: no limit. Default: below the open-files limit read at start (RLIMIT_NOFILE), with room for the process's own files and sockets (S3, databases, admin port): the limit minus 1000, or half of it when it is under 4000. Without it, a client that holds enough connections (5 addresses at the per-address limit, or one with a password and a few databases) runs the process out of open files
      --max-unauth-conns-per-ip <MAX_UNAUTH_CONNS_PER_IP>
          Connections at once from one address that have not authenticated (0: no limit). Further connections are closed at once. A connection stops counting when it authenticates, and counts again if it logs out of every database. A driver keeps two such connections per client (monitoring and round-trip time), which never authenticate, and every new connection counts here until its authentication: the default leaves room for about 1,900 clients (for example warm serverless functions) behind one address. Measured: with 1000, 1000 clients behind one address do not start [default: 4000]
      --max-conns-per-db <MAX_CONNS_PER_DB>
          Authenticated connections at once on one database, from every address (0: no limit). An authentication that would go beyond it is refused (the connection stays open, not authenticated). A connection authenticated on a database counts once, whatever the number of its users there [default: 5000]
      --handshake-timeout-secs <HANDSHAKE_TIMEOUT_SECS>
          The TLS handshake and the first message must arrive within this many seconds of the connection, and before authentication (with --auth) every message must arrive whole within it once its first byte has (0: off) [default: 10]
      --unauth-idle-timeout-secs <UNAUTH_IDLE_TIMEOUT_SECS>
          With --auth, a connection that has not authenticated (or has logged out of every database) and sends nothing for this many seconds is closed (0: off). A driver's monitoring connections, which never authenticate, send a hello at least every ~10 s (heartbeatFrequencyMS) and are not touched [default: 120]
      --pre-auth-max-message-bytes <PRE_AUTH_MAX_MESSAGE_BYTES>
          Largest message (bytes, also after decompression) accepted before a connection has authenticated (with --auth) [default: 65536]
      --ip-allowlist-refresh-secs <IP_ALLOWLIST_REFRESH_SECS>
          A database's allow list is re-read from its metadata at most this often (changes made by this process apply at once) [default: 5]
      --ipv6-group-prefix <IPV6_GROUP_PREFIX>
          IPv6 addresses are counted and limited by this prefix (one /64 is usually one client) [default: 64]
      --netguard-max-tracked <NETGUARD_MAX_TRACKED>
          Most client addresses whose failures are tracked at once (memory bound) [default: 100000]
      --netguard-max-dbs-per-ip <NETGUARD_MAX_DBS_PER_IP>
          Most databases whose failures are tracked at once for one address (memory bound); beyond it, failures on further databases count only toward the per-address threshold [default: 1000]
      --auth
          Require authentication and authorization for every command (mongod's --auth)
      --grantable-roles <GRANTABLE_ROLES>
          With --auth: the only roles a caller that holds neither root nor clusterAdmin (a provisioner, a customer's user administrator) may hand out with createUser, updateUser and grantRolesToUser, comma-separated, e.g. `readWrite,read`. When set, such a caller may manage users only on customer databases (never admin, local, config, $external), may grant only the listed built-in roles of the database the user is defined on, never one of its own roles, and may not create or change roles. Only built-in roles of one database without user administration are accepted (read, readWrite, dbAdmin). Empty: no restriction (mongod's rules) [default: ""]
      --tls-mode <TLS_MODE>
          TLS on the client port: disabled, allowTLS, preferTLS or requireTLS (mongod's net.tls.mode) [default: disabled]
      --tls-certificate-key-file <TLS_CERTIFICATE_KEY_FILE>
          PEM file with the server certificate chain and its private key (net.tls.certificateKeyFile) [default: ""]
      --tls-ca-file <TLS_CA_FILE>
          PEM file with the CA certificates client certificates must chain to (net.tls.CAFile) [default: ""]
